title: Main ideas and summaries
intro: Find the controlling idea without mistaking a vivid detail for the whole passage. Learn the evidence process, study six worked examples, and test it on three new passages.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map

sections.heading: Find the controlling idea, not just the subject
body: A passage’s subject is the thing it discusses: a bus pilot, a family desk, a research method, or a renovation. Its controlling idea is what the passage develops about that subject. Saying this passage is about buses will not distinguish a report that proves profitability from one that gathers promising evidence while limiting its claims. Start with a subject-and-movement sentence: the town uses a limited trial to decide what it still needs to learn. That sentence captures both the topic and the direction of the discussion.

Look at the opening problem and the closing resolution, but do not assume the last sentence alone contains the answer. The middle paragraphs explain how the passage reaches its ending. A narrative can move from an expectation to a changed understanding without announcing a moral. An informational passage may qualify an initial interpretation rather than replace it completely. Notice contrasts such as at first, yet, instead, and still. They often mark the relationship that a correct main-idea answer must preserve.

examples.text:
Mara had expected her grandmother’s desk to contain something impressive: the letters of a celebrated traveler, perhaps, or the plans for a house never built. Instead she found grocery lists. Dates ran across the tops in an increasingly uneven hand. Beside “pears,” on one list, her grandmother had written “Mara likes the green ones.”

Her brother suggested recycling the papers. The desk was going to a neighbor, and neither of them wanted another box in an already crowded apartment. Mara agreed that they could not preserve everything. She set aside the advertisements, the duplicate receipts, and three envelopes that held nothing. But she slipped the pear list into her coat pocket.

On the way home she stopped at the corner shop. For years she had bought whichever fruit cost least, making purchases as efficiently as possible. That evening she stood before the pears longer than she needed to. The green ones were not on sale. She chose two anyway, then laughed at herself for expecting them to taste different. When she reached home, she placed the list beside the fruit rather than filing it away.

Question: The passage primarily traces Mara’s discovery that:

Supported answer: an ordinary object can preserve a personal connection

Reason: The list’s small note about Mara changes her attitude toward an ordinary purchase, and she displays it beside the pears. The supported answer is “an ordinary object can preserve a personal connection.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

examples.text:
A local museum displayed a map assembled from residents’ childhood recollections. Volunteers asked participants to mark places they remembered visiting before age twelve. The completed map included a dense cluster of swimming spots along the eastern riverbank and only two marks in the west of town.

At first the curator thought this distribution reflected where children had played. Then she examined the interview list. Most participants had grown up in the eastern neighborhoods. The memories represented this particular group rather than the town as a whole. The curator matched the marks to the interview records. Several dots that appeared to show separate swimming places came from friends describing the same stretch of river. A crowded part of the map could therefore reflect a well-connected group as much as a busy childhood destination. Nor could an empty part tell her which places western residents would have named if they had been asked. The map had not been designed to sample the town evenly: volunteers had recruited acquaintances and people who attended the museum’s weekend events.

The curator kept the map on display but changed its caption. Instead of “Where our town’s children played,” it now read “Places remembered by this group of residents.” She invited people from the west to add recollections to a second map, preserving the first map and its interview list as a record of the original project. The western blank areas were not evidence that children had never played there. They were, she wrote, an invitation to ask whose memories had yet to be included.

Question: The passage mainly describes a curator’s effort to:

Supported answer: make a memory map’s claim match the people actually represented

Reason: She revises the caption and seeks additional memories after noticing the uneven participant pool. The supported answer is “make a memory map’s claim match the people actually represented.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

sections.heading: Match a summary to the passage’s full movement
body: A strong summary includes the major stages in proportion to their importance. For the map passage, the curator first treats the distribution as a town-wide picture, discovers an uneven participant pool, revises the claim, and invites additional residents. The controlling movement is making the display’s claim fit the evidence while broadening participation. A choice about swimming locations repeats a detail but does not summarize that movement. A choice about discarding memories reverses the actual solution, which preserves the original project and documents its limits.

Test your proposed summary against each paragraph. It should explain why the major paragraphs belong together without listing every object or name. If one paragraph challenges the result, a summary that presents the result as settled is incomplete. If the passage retains a useful method while acknowledging limitations, a summary claiming total rejection goes too far. Compress the passage into a relationship, not a catalogue. Words such as evaluates, revises, distinguishes, and comes to recognize often express movement more accurately than celebrates or proves when the passage is cautious.

examples.text:
Passage A — Theater director
Our theater’s facade is intact, but the stage rigging is unsafe. Preserving the room exactly as it stood in 1930 would make it impossible to use. I want to retain the painted ceiling and the worn foyer steps while replacing the cables above the stage. A public building survives through repeated encounters. A locked theater is a photograph of itself.

Passage B — Architectural historian
Use can help preserve a theater, but “modernization” is sometimes a generous word for erasure. The original stage equipment reveals how productions were mounted; removing all of it would sever that record. I support new safety systems, provided representative old mechanisms remain visible and the alterations are documented. Preservation need not mean freezing a building. It means knowing what changes cost.

Both writers are responding to a proposed renovation. Neither disputes that the existing rigging is unsafe. The debate concerns how to change the theater while retaining what makes its past legible.

Question: Taken together, the passages chiefly examine:

Supported answer: how a theater can remain usable while preserving evidence of its history

Reason: Both writers accept safety changes and debate what should remain during renovation. The supported answer is “how a theater can remain usable while preserving evidence of its history.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

examples.text:
Researchers placed sticky collection cards at three distances from a stand of trees to learn where its seeds traveled. Each card remained outdoors for the same week. Cards nearest the trees caught the most seeds; cards farthest away caught fewer. A student proposed using the pattern to estimate the distance traveled by a typical seed.

The lead researcher urged caution. A card could catch only seeds that struck its surface. A seed crossing the area above a card would not be counted. Heavy rain midway through the week had also washed material from two cards, which the team marked as damaged. The remaining cards offered evidence about the collected seeds, but not a complete inventory of every seed dispersed.

The team planned a second collection period with protected cards and observations of wind direction. It would compare patterns across the two weeks instead of treating the first week as a final answer. One researcher described the cards as “windows onto a moving process.” A window could reveal something real, she said, without showing the whole landscape.

Question: The passage’s main purpose is to explain:

Supported answer: why seed collection results must be interpreted in light of what the method can capture

Reason: The researcher distinguishes collected seeds from all dispersed seeds and proposes additional observation. The supported answer is “why seed collection results must be interpreted in light of what the method can capture.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

sections.heading: Reject narrow, inflated, and imported choices
body: Three recurring main-idea traps deserve separate tests. A narrow choice describes one vivid example and cannot account for the rest of the text. An inflated choice changes a local event into a universal lesson or turns a tentative result into proof. An imported choice makes a plausible claim about the subject that the passage never develops. The correct answer must be supported by the particular passage, even when another choice sounds wiser, more scientific, or more inspirational in ordinary conversation.

For each remaining option, identify its scope and attitude. Does it refer to the interviewed residents or all children in town? Does it say the service is promising or permanently successful? Does it say the narrator changes a belief or abandons the activity entirely? These are not cosmetic differences. They determine whether the choice can survive the passage’s explicit qualifications. A correct summary can sound modest because the evidence is modest. Do not reward a dramatic answer merely because the passage contains an emotionally memorable final image.

examples.text:
A town introduced a Saturday bus between the library and three neighborhoods. Before the pilot, residents at public meetings had asked for daily service. The transport office could initially fund only eight Saturdays. It counted riders and invited anonymous comments after each trip.

The first Saturday drew twelve passengers. By the eighth, twenty-nine people rode. Several comments praised the library stop; others asked for an earlier departure. One resident wrote that the trip was useful but too infrequent for a weekday job. A council member called the growing attendance encouraging. The office’s report used a more guarded phrase: the figures supported continuing the trial, not yet expanding it to every day.

The report noted two limits. The trial took place during a summer reading program, and it did not measure how many riders would pay a fare. The office proposed another eight weeks after the program ended, with an optional fare question on the comment card. The council approved the additional trial without promising a permanent route.

Question: The passage’s main point is that the town:

Supported answer: is using a promising bus pilot to gather evidence before making a larger commitment

Reason: Rider numbers rise, but the report proposes further testing because demand under different conditions remains uncertain. The supported answer is “is using a promising bus pilot to gather evidence before making a larger commitment.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

sections.heading: Treat narrative change as evidence, not a slogan
body: In literary narrative, track the starting belief, the complicating event, and the final action. Mara initially expects impressive documents, discovers a small note showing personal attention, and later displays that note beside the fruit. The ending supports a connection through an ordinary object. It does not prove she will preserve every family possession or stop comparing prices forever. The final action matters because it differs from her initial expectations; the meaning emerges through that contrast.

A narrator’s attitude can be mixed. Enjoying an interruption while worrying about rehearsal time does not mean the narrator dislikes music or resents the aunt completely. A main-idea choice should preserve the development across those mixed responses. Distinguish what a character learns from what an author claims about everyone. Before choosing a broad lesson, point to at least two moments in the narrative that support it. Then remove any universal language that those moments cannot justify. This keeps interpretation anchored in change actually shown on the page.

examples.text:

This time Nico stayed under the bridge. He noticed water striking a loose piece of timber, a bicycle chain clicking above him, and pauses in which the river seemed louder than the road. He began recording only after the ten minutes had passed.

The supported answer is “learns that patient attention can change his experience of a familiar place.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Give the first read a purpose: learn enough structure to locate evidence efficiently. After reading a question, name the task before examining its choices. Is it asking for an explicit detail, an inference, a word’s local meaning, a paragraph’s function, or a relationship between sources? Different tasks require different evidence. A detail usually sends you back to a narrow location; a summary needs the passage’s controlling movement. Rereading the entire passage for every question hides this difference and consumes time without guaranteeing a better decision.

If two choices remain, compare them against the same piece of evidence. Ask which word in each choice creates the disagreement. The decisive difference is often scope, certainty, chronology, speaker, or purpose rather than an unfamiliar vocabulary word. A choice saying every participant is not interchangeable with one saying the interviewed group. Identify the mismatch in a short phrase. If you cannot locate support after a deliberate attempt, select the best available answer, flag it, and move. Use a later return to test one unresolved issue rather than restart the question from nothing.

At each passage transition, check elapsed time and unanswered items. Reserving a brief final review is useful only if you have selected answers throughout the section. This practice lab records raw accuracy on original material; it cannot promise a particular ACT scaled score. Your score goal should guide careful review of repeated errors, not encourage claims that a small practice set predicts a thirty-six. Build speed from a consistent evidence process, then examine whether timing or comprehension changes when you use complete forty-minute forms.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: Before revealing an explanation, record a specific confidence judgment. Afterward, compare your chosen answer with the actual evidence rather than simply reading why the key is correct. Write the smallest rule that would have changed your decision: return to the stated date, separate the quoted speaker from the author, reject a claim about every resident, or compare proportions using the same denominator. A note such as read more carefully is too broad to guide another attempt. Name the exact decision you made and the evidence you overlooked.

Use the error-cause control to distinguish content or comprehension gaps from timing, a misread stem, a rushed choice, or uncertainty between two options. A slow correct answer can still reveal a weak process, while a quick wrong answer can reveal unjustified confidence. Review at least one tempting distractor and explain its defect using the passage. If the explanation sounds equally applicable to every wrong choice, make it more concrete. The point is to acquire a transferable check, not memorize which letter happened to be right in one question.

After the repair, do a fresh set rather than immediately repeating the same remembered item. Keep full-section questions separate from topic drills so the timed result measures a new decision. This lab saves completed practice to your signed-in account and shows mastery only after sufficient distinct-question evidence. A topic badge is a signal about this bank, not proof of an official scaled score. When today’s plan exceeds the available budget, unfinished tasks remain visible and carry forward in order; extra work should be a deliberate choice rather than an invisible doubling of tomorrow’s assignment.

sections.heading: Turn the stem into a precise search
body: An explicit-detail question asks what the passage states, but the answer may use a paraphrase rather than identical words. First identify the requested fact: who acted, what happened, when it happened, why the text says it happened, or what a named measurement counts. Use the question’s distinctive noun or event to find the relevant paragraph. Read the surrounding sentence too; a phrase quoted correctly can still be attached to the wrong person or stage of the story.

In the bus passage, asking why the report mentions the summer program requires the sentence naming the limits of the trial. The program may have affected demand. It is not evidence that every future route is funded, because the passage never makes that financial claim. Paraphrase the located evidence in your own words before checking the options. This small step keeps a familiar-looking choice from displacing the actual relationship you just found. Exact evidence takes priority over a plausible general explanation.

sections.heading: Separate sequence from cause
body: An event occurring after another event does not automatically mean the first caused the second. Detail questions sometimes ask for the order of events, while other questions ask for a cause explicitly supplied by the passage. Keep those tasks separate. In a pilot that adds an evening return window and reminder messages at the same time, improved returns follow both changes. The passage can report that sequence without assigning the entire improvement to either change alone.

Build a quick sequence when dates or stages matter: initial expectation, trial, observation, revised report, further test. Then examine causal language. Because, led to, and attributed to can establish a stated explanation; coincided with marks a weaker relationship. A choice may preserve the right events but reverse their order or strengthen coincidence into proof. When the stem asks according to the passage, report the text’s claim faithfully even if you personally think another explanation is likely. Your outside knowledge cannot supply a causal statement the writer did not make.

sections.heading: Control the unit, speaker, and condition
body: A detail’s unit is part of the fact. A tool-return count measures tools, not borrowers. Occupied seats at two times do not count distinct visitors over the whole afternoon. A map assembled from volunteer participants reflects that group, not automatically every resident. Before accepting a number or comparison, identify what is counted, over which period, and under what conditions. These qualifiers often do more work than the number itself.

Also track speakers. A visitor may propose a strong interpretation that the researchers immediately qualify; the passage does not thereby endorse the visitor’s claim. A director and a historian can agree about unsafe rigging while disagreeing about retained machinery. When an option says the report, the historian, or the narrator believes something, check that speaker specifically. An accurate sentence from Passage A is not necessarily an accurate description of Passage B. Underline the attribution mentally and reread the sentence where the opinion appears.

sections.heading: Check a paraphrase without demanding identical wording
body: The right answer may translate a stated phrase into simpler language. A report’s guarded wording can mean that evidence supports continuing a trial without justifying daily expansion. The passage need not use the exact word cautious for that paraphrase to be correct. Match the relationship and strength of the claim, not merely repeated vocabulary. Conversely, an option can borrow several words from the passage and connect them in a way the text never does.

Cross-reference the relevant paragraph in each text. If an option relies entirely on Passage A, it cannot establish agreement unless Passage B also supports it. If the stem asks how one passage extends another, identify the new consideration and the common starting point. Future researchers valuing currently distracting sounds extends the engineer’s concern about visible choices because it explains why alternatives must remain available. This relationship is more specific than both discuss recordings, which names a subject without showing how the arguments connect.

examples.text:
Passage A — Theater director
Our theater’s facade is intact, but the stage rigging is unsafe. Preserving the room exactly as it stood in 1930 would make it impossible to use. I want to retain the painted ceiling and the worn foyer steps while replacing the cables above the stage. A public building survives through repeated encounters. A locked theater is a photograph of itself.

Passage B — Architectural historian
Use can help preserve a theater, but “modernization” is sometimes a generous word for erasure. The original stage equipment reveals how productions were mounted; removing all of it would sever that record. I support new safety systems, provided representative old mechanisms remain visible and the alterations are documented. Preservation need not mean freezing a building. It means knowing what changes cost.

Both writers are responding to a proposed renovation. Neither disputes that the existing rigging is unsafe. The debate concerns how to change the theater while retaining what makes its past legible.

Question: Which claim would both writers most likely accept?

Supported answer: Preservation can allow changes that make the theater safe to use

Reason: The director wants cable replacement; the historian explicitly supports new safety systems. They differ about retained evidence, not the need for safe use. The supported answer is “Preservation can allow changes that make the theater safe to use.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 2: Two Ways to Keep a Theater

examples.text:
Researchers placed sticky collection cards at three distances from a stand of trees to learn where its seeds traveled. Each card remained outdoors for the same week. Cards nearest the trees caught the most seeds; cards farthest away caught fewer. A student proposed using the pattern to estimate the distance traveled by a typical seed.

The lead researcher urged caution. A card could catch only seeds that struck its surface. A seed crossing the area above a card would not be counted. Heavy rain midway through the week had also washed material from two cards, which the team marked as damaged. The remaining cards offered evidence about the collected seeds, but not a complete inventory of every seed dispersed.

The team planned a second collection period with protected cards and observations of wind direction. It would compare patterns across the two weeks instead of treating the first week as a final answer. One researcher described the cards as “windows onto a moving process.” A window could reveal something real, she said, without showing the whole landscape.

Question: Taken together, the near/far counts and the methodological limits support which statement?

Supported answer: The collected sample varies with distance, but it cannot establish every seed’s travel distance

Reason: The observed distance pattern concerns collected seeds; missed trajectories and damaged cards prevent a census of total dispersal. The supported answer is “The collected sample varies with distance, but it cannot establish every seed’s travel distance.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 6: Seeds on the Wind

sections.heading: Read the graphic’s labels before its pattern
body: A visual-information item requires the passage and graphic together. Start with the title, axes or column labels, units, time period, and category definitions. An occupied-seat count is not a unique-visitor count. A tool-return percentage uses scheduled returns as the denominator, not the number of volunteers. When a row shows eighty-one on-time returns out of ninety scheduled returns, the proportion is ninety percent. Eighty-one is a count; it becomes a percent only after division by the stated total.

Before comparing periods, ask whether denominators or measurement conditions changed. A raw increase can coexist with a smaller rate, and a rate increase need not isolate a cause. The passage may identify reminders, weather, or seasonality as simultaneous changes. Use the graphic to establish the numerical pattern and the prose to establish what that pattern can reasonably mean. If the chart cannot count distinct people, no clever calculation creates that missing measure. Reject answers that change the unit or treat an association as experimental proof.

examples.text:
A town introduced a Saturday bus between the library and three neighborhoods. Before the pilot, residents at public meetings had asked for daily service. The transport office could initially fund only eight Saturdays. It counted riders and invited anonymous comments after each trip.

The first Saturday drew twelve passengers. By the eighth, twenty-nine people rode. Several comments praised the library stop; others asked for an earlier departure. One resident wrote that the trip was useful but too infrequent for a weekday job. A council member called the growing attendance encouraging. The office’s report used a more guarded phrase: the figures supported continuing the trial, not yet expanding it to every day.

The report noted two limits. The trial took place during a summer reading program, and it did not measure how many riders would pay a fare. The office proposed another eight weeks after the program ended, with an optional fare question on the comment card. The council approved the additional trial without promising a permanent route.

Question: How do the rider counts and the report’s qualifications work together?

Supported answer: They provide a positive signal while identifying questions the counts alone cannot answer

Reason: The numbers support further trial service; the qualifications concern seasonality and willingness to pay, which the counts do not measure. The supported answer is “They provide a positive signal while identifying questions the counts alone cannot answer.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 3: The Bus Pilot

sections.heading: Keep a combined conclusion within all supplied limits
body: Integration questions often tempt you with a true-looking sentence that ignores a qualification elsewhere. A table may show fewer unfilled requests, while the text explains that it counts only requests blocked by tools still out. You can conclude that this type of request decreased during the trial. You cannot conclude that every requested tool was available or that the library should stop purchasing tools. The combined answer must satisfy the graphic’s definitions and the passage’s scope simultaneously.

For a final check, make a two-column mental audit: what the source shows, and what it does not show. A clear image can illustrate root growth without representing all plots; two library seat observations can show occupancy at those times without measuring an afternoon’s unique visitors. In paired texts, apply the same discipline to authors’ positions. Mark the evidence supporting the shared claim and the condition that limits it. A careful synthesis usually retains those conditions, even if a broader answer sounds more decisive.

examples.text:
Nico spent the first morning of the sound workshop recording traffic. The instructor asked him to choose a location and listen there for ten minutes before touching the recorder. He picked the bridge because he knew what he would hear: engines, tires, horns. He pressed the recording button after less than a minute.

When the instructor played his clip, the traffic filled every second. “You found what you expected,” she said. She sent him back without suggesting a different location. This time Nico stayed under the bridge. He noticed water striking a loose piece of timber, a bicycle chain clicking above him, and pauses in which the river seemed louder than the road. He began recording only after the ten minutes had passed.

That afternoon he compared the clips. The second still contained engines; listening had not removed them. But it also held the soft intervals he had missed. He labeled the first file “Bridge” and hesitated over the second. Finally he gave both files the same name and added only the dates. The place had not changed enough to explain the difference.

Question: What is the relationship between the instructor’s first comment and Nico’s final reflection?

Supported answer: Both connect the recordings to the listener’s expectations and attention

Reason: “You found what you expected” and the final observation that the place had barely changed point toward the listener’s role. The supported answer is “Both connect the recordings to the listener’s expectations and attention.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 4: Listening Beneath the Bridge

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Give the first read a purpose: learn enough structure to locate evidence efficiently. After reading a question, name the task before examining its choices. Is it asking for an explicit detail, an inference, a word’s local meaning, a paragraph’s function, or a relationship between sources? Different tasks require different evidence. A detail usually sends you back to a narrow location; a summary needs the passage’s controlling movement. Rereading the entire passage for every question hides this difference and consumes time without guaranteeing a better decision.

If two choices remain, compare them against the same piece of evidence. Ask which word in each choice creates the disagreement. The decisive difference is often scope, certainty, chronology, speaker, or purpose rather than an unfamiliar vocabulary word. A choice saying every participant is not interchangeable with one saying the interviewed group. Identify the mismatch in a short phrase. If you cannot locate support after a deliberate attempt, select the best available answer, flag it, and move. Use a later return to test one unresolved issue rather than restart the question from nothing.

At each passage transition, check elapsed time and unanswered items. Reserving a brief final review is useful only if you have selected answers throughout the section. This practice lab records raw accuracy on original material; it cannot promise a particular ACT scaled score. Your score goal should guide careful review of repeated errors, not encourage claims that a small practice set predicts a thirty-six. Build speed from a consistent evidence process, then examine whether timing or comprehension changes when you use complete forty-minute forms.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: Before revealing an explanation, record a specific confidence judgment. Afterward, compare your chosen answer with the actual evidence rather than simply reading why the key is correct. Write the smallest rule that would have changed your decision: return to the stated date, separate the quoted speaker from the author, reject a claim about every resident, or compare proportions using the same denominator. A note such as read more carefully is too broad to guide another attempt. Name the exact decision you made and the evidence you overlooked.

Use the error-cause control to distinguish content or comprehension gaps from timing, a misread stem, a rushed choice, or uncertainty between two options. A slow correct answer can still reveal a weak process, while a quick wrong answer can reveal unjustified confidence. Review at least one tempting distractor and explain its defect using the passage. If the explanation sounds equally applicable to every wrong choice, make it more concrete. The point is to acquire a transferable check, not memorize which letter happened to be right in one question.

After the repair, do a fresh set rather than immediately repeating the same remembered item. Keep full-section questions separate from topic drills so the timed result measures a new decision. This lab saves completed practice to your signed-in account and shows mastery only after sufficient distinct-question evidence. A topic badge is a signal about this bank, not proof of an official scaled score. When today’s plan exceeds the available budget, unfinished tasks remain visible and carry forward in order; extra work should be a deliberate choice rather than an invisible doubling of tomorrow’s assignment.

choices: Only the smoothest version should survive
Future listeners must ask today’s exact questions
A useful listening copy should be accompanied by access to evidence about its production
All processing is inherently unacceptable

choices: It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence
It denies that anyone should enter the theater
It proves that every old mechanism is safe
It treats documentation as a replacement for all surviving features

The supported answer is “It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
